heading: 6. SEKI+ and SEKI
question: besogo prints S[SEKI+] as a seki in sente and S[SEKI] as one in gote, and ranks SEKI+ higher for the solver, whether it kills or lives. The checker reads SEKI+ as a seki in which the solver keeps sente: at the leaf the solver may play elsewhere, or the opponent must answer first. Is that your meaning? And on the leaves where your tree and the checker disagree, which label is right?

options.label: SEKI+: the solver keeps sente
options.meaning: The checker's reading (design D11). With the solver to play, SEKI+ when it may play elsewhere and the seki holds (Diagram 1); with the opponent to play, when the opponent must answer, because otherwise the solver kills or lives without seki (Diagram 5). Everything else is SEKI, also a seki the opponent could still improve by a ko if the solver played elsewhere (Diagram 3). besogo ranks SEKI+ higher, so where the solver's sibling moves reach both, only the SEKI+ moves are correct (Diagram 2). In your trees this reading moves a grade only in Problem 15418, and there only if its leaf 3 is not SEKI+ as well.

options.label: SEKI+ only with the solver to play
options.meaning: The + only on a seki whose line ends with the opponent's move. A leaf where the opponent must still answer is then SEKI, as in Problem 1862 (Diagram 5) and four more of your leaves, all in trees that use no +. Your three S[SEKI+] leaves with the opponent to play, in Problems 13872, 2049 and 2248, lose their +; that changes no grade.

options.label: No + from the checker
options.meaning: The checker tells a seki from life and death but does not compare SEKI with SEKI+: your + stays as you wrote it, and so does the grading.

recommendation: SEKI+: the solver keeps sente. Where your trees use the +, they use it this way. Problem 2521 splits the two labels as both readings do (Diagrams 1 and 2), and your three S[SEKI+] leaves with the opponent to play, in Problems 13872, 2049 and 2248, are sekis the opponent must still answer, which only this reading allows. In the trees that use the +, the checker agrees with 30 of the 32 leaves it decides. Per leaf: keep 2521; S[SEKI] for 1881 leaves 2 and 4; S[ALIVE] for 2089 leaf 2; S[SEKI+] for 1862 leaf 1, if trees that use no + should get it too. None of these changes a grade.
text: Your trees mark 37 leaves S[SEKI+], in 28 problems, and 185 leaves S[SEKI], in 86; only four problems use both. besogo's editor offers the + as a sente box on a seki, and prints SEKI+ as in sente and SEKI as in gote. It ranks SEKI+ above SEKI for the solver whether the problem is to kill or to live, so the sente is always the solver's.

The checker calls a leaf a seki when the target lives whatever the ko threats, but cannot live without seki when the attacker has every threat. For the sente it plays one forced pass. With the solver to play, the solver passes, and the seki must still hold even when the opponent has four ko threats. With the opponent to play, the opponent passes, and the solver, with four ko threats, must then kill or live without seki. The checks with a forced pass under the diagrams are such searches; where a check says a seki counts as dead, only life without seki counts.

These tests needed one fix, found in this review and now made in the checker. When a position repeats, the solver counts a cycle of plain captures, as in sending two and returning one, as a seki. Where a seki counts as dead, it still counted such a cycle as life, so a group that could only force a repetition passed for alive. Now every repetition counts as a kill wherever a seki counts as dead: that changed 30 rows of the table, each with a note of what the checker said before. The positions shown keep their classes, and so does every check under the diagrams that counts a seki as dead.

A pass is not the only way to keep sente: the solver may still have a forcing move. So we also followed the forcing moves, up to two deep: a move of the solver that the opponent must answer, then every answer that keeps the seki. On all 128 leaves where both tests are decided, the answer is the same as with the single pass.

The table lists every SEKI+ and SEKI leaf. The checker searched its own area at 200,000 nodes per search, and the leaves left undecided once more at 2,000,000. Of your 37 SEKI+ leaves, it says SEKI+ on 27 and SEKI on 2, and 8 stay undecided. Of your 185 SEKI leaves, it says SEKI on 61, SEKI+ on 41, ALIVE on 7, DEAD on 1 and KO on 1, and 74 stay undecided.

The disagreements are of three kinds. 41 of your SEKI leaves are seki in the solver's sente: either the opponent must still answer (Diagram 5, and Problems 9, 1733, 15418 and 15454), or the solver may play elsewhere (36 leaves). All of them are in trees that use no +, so there your SEKI may only mean that the + was not considered. In the four trees that use both labels, the checker agrees with every leaf it decides.

Two of your SEKI+ leaves are seki in gote, 1881 leaves 2 and 4: if Black plays elsewhere there, White lives without seki, by a ko in leaf 2 (Diagram 3) and at once in leaf 4. And seven of your SEKI leaves are no seki: the target lives without one (Diagram 8). Two more are a kill and a ko (7487 leaves 73 and 76). We read the four leaves shown move by move; the other verdicts in the table are the checker's alone.

Most of these changes move no grade, because the seki is not the best result of its branch. The ones that do are not about the +: with the checker's decided classes in place of your labels, grading changes in Problems 2390 (Black's D19 at move 1 becomes wrong) and 7487 (Black's A16 at move 3 becomes correct), where your SEKI is life or a kill. Of the + changes, only 15418's can move a grade: Black's A16 at move 1 becomes wrong, unless leaf 3 is SEKI+ too, which the checker says unless its open clean-result test makes it a ko.

Your trees have no leaf marked DSKO or ASKO, so superko has no example here. The checker tests for it only when a proof had to decide a repeated position, and marks any DSKO or ASKO it finds as unverified. On these 222 leaves it found none; the test stayed undecided on four.

positions.heading: Problem 2521, leaves 1 and 3: your SEKI+ and your SEKI in one tree
text: Both lines end in a seki. In leaf 1 White makes the last move, and Black may play elsewhere; in leaf 3 Black makes it, and White may. Your tree marks the first S[SEKI+] and the second S[SEKI], as the checker reads them, and besogo grades by it: Black 1 in Diagram 2 is wrong only because its seki ends in gote.

diagrams.caption: Leaf 1, marked S[SEKI+]. White 4 is the last move of the seki, and Black may play elsewhere.
Leaf 3, marked S[SEKI]. Black 5 is the last move, and White may play elsewhere: even with a free move, Black cannot live without the seki.

positions.heading: Problem 1881, leaf 2: S[SEKI+], but Black must still connect
text: Black's three stones in the corner hold White to a seki, but the seki is not finished. If Black plays elsewhere now, White can fight a ko to live without seki (Diagram 3). Black 7 in Diagram 4 connects, and then White may play elsewhere: the seki ends in Black's gote, so the checker says SEKI. Leaf 4, also marked S[SEKI+], is this corner without Black 3 and White 4, and the checker says SEKI there too.

diagrams.caption: Leaf 2, marked S[SEKI+], with Black to play. If Black plays elsewhere, White can fight a ko to live without seki, and Black needs one threat more than White to stop it.
Black 7 connects. Now White may play elsewhere: even with a free move and four ko threats, Black cannot kill.

positions.heading: Problem 1862, leaf 1: S[SEKI], but White must answer
text: Black 1 makes the seki and threatens more: if White plays elsewhere, Black lives without seki (Diagram 6). After White's answer in Diagram 7, Black may play elsewhere, so Black keeps sente and the checker says SEKI+. Leaf 1 of Problem 13872 is the same case, and there your tree has S[SEKI+]; the tree of 1862 uses no + at all.

diagrams.caption: Leaf 1, marked S[SEKI], with White to play. If White plays elsewhere, Black lives without seki, so White must answer.
White 2 plays elsewhere, and Black 3 puts the three White stones inside in atari: Black captures them and lives without seki.
White 2 answers. Now Black may play elsewhere: the seki ends in Black's sente.

positions.heading: Problem 2089, leaf 2: S[SEKI], but White lives
text: Black 1 and Black 3 are dead inside White's corner: White lives with Black to play, and can capture them whenever it needs to (Diagram 9). A seki needed a different White 4, such as C18 (Diagram 10). The checker says ALIVE, the stronger claim: White lives without seki even when Black has every ko threat.

diagrams.caption: Leaf 2, marked S[SEKI], with Black to play. White 4 lives, and Black 1 and Black 3 are dead.
Black 5 is no help: after White 6, Black's three stones have one liberty left and cannot escape.
White 4 here instead would allow a seki.
